world.title: El Niño probability above 95%: Find out what it means for farmers
world.description: South African farmers should prepare for a hotter, drier summer as the probability of El Niño conditions developing has risen above 95%. A South African Weather Service presentation at the Sernick Emerging Farmer’s Day on 7 August projects a “very strong” El Niño, with sea surface temperature anomalies reaching +2.9°C by October to December. Below-normal rainfall is expected to spread across most of the country by summer, raising the risk of agricultural drought, declining soil moisture and livestock heat stress. However, better soil moisture and healthy dam levels after two La Niña seasons offer some buffer.

science.description: Tropical forests store enormous amounts of carbon and harbor most of the world's terrestrial biodiversity, but scientists fear that increasingly severe droughts threaten their ability to survive and continue absorbing carbon from the atmosphere. A new study published in Nature offers unexpected hope, however, and shows that tropical trees may be more adaptable to drought than scientists had previously believed.

science.title: Mirage or miracle? JWST finds earliest known 'black hole star' at cosmic dawn
science.description: Little red dots have puzzled astronomers since their discovery in James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) data from the universe's deep past. Their "powering engines" might resemble a newly discovered phenomenon dubbed a "black hole star"—an early, rapidly growing black hole wrapped in dense gas. This object, described in a study published today in Nature by researchers at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) and international collaborators, may help explain how billion-solar-mass black holes formed so soon after the Big Bang.

science.title: When male suitors abound, female treefrogs have trouble picking mates
science.description: Much like an indecisive single person on a dating app, female treefrogs struggle to pick the most desirable mates when they have too many options to choose from. According to a new study published Aug. 12 in the journal iScience, when female Cope's gray treefrogs gather around ponds during mating season to listen to large groups of males chirping in noisy "choruses," they struggle to pick the most desirable male. The researchers call this phenomenon "choice overload," and it may affect the way species evolve over time.
